evidence: Draft (one sentence): "Make sure you're in a safe place to do this." It is the same string the_change names (Emulate, samples cm and co, word for word) and it appears once in CONTEXT.txt, as the first sentence of the safety paragraph. SOURCE: it replaces "Put yourself in a place where you can safely do this."; the meaning to keep is the published guide's "Choose a physically secure place without driving, water, machinery, or anyone needing your supervision." The instruction is the same (be somewhere safe for this). The specifics of the published line (driving, water, machinery, people needing attention) are carried by the very next sentence in the context, "Don't do this if you're driving, in the water, operating machinery, or otherwise need to be attending to yourself or other people.", which the swap does not touch, so "safe" reads as physical safety. No claim, fact, number or first-person statement is added. In context: "this" points to the session the section is preparing, the same antecedent as "How long do you want to spend on this?" earlier in the section and as in the sentence it replaces. It opens a new paragraph, so the move from planning the session to safety is marked by the break and it follows. One thing I looked at hard: the previous paragraph ends "Make sure you're leaving some time at the end to come back...", so two "Make sure you're" openers sit either side of the paragraph break, and "make sure you can change state" comes two paragraphs later (a T26 candidate; the replaced sentence had none of these, so the swap adds the second of the three). I read them as the section's own idiom for pre-flight checks: parallel items on one list, in a casual voice that suits a "Before you begin" section, and a plain idiom rather than a distinctive phrase, so the repetition marks list items and is not an echo that does nothing. Minor, not a failure. Tells: I went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the draft in its context and none is actually happening. T02: the neighbouring sentences are a run of safety conditions, but they are full sentences of different lengths with different specifics, that run is the source's own shape (a safety checklist where each condition is a different case), and the swap adds no step to it, since the replaced sentence was an imperative in the same slot. T14 and T15: nothing is moved or reordered, and the new wording is the more common phrase, not a rarer one swapped in. T19: it is a rule whose reason follows, not an announcement. T06: "safe place" is made concrete by the next sentence. C02: no stray pronoun; C03 and C04: no first-person fact and no outside claim. Linter findings: "D9 follows the source order" is a one-sentence swap in the same slot doing the same job, so following the source's order is trivial; nothing is reordered and one imperative does not engage T13 or T09; accepted. "E36/E41 heavy second person" (10.0 per 100) is one "you're" in a ten-word sentence; the guide's safety steps are directions to the reader and the replaced sentence also addressed "you", so the context answers it; accepted. Side note that does not affect the verdict: the writer's ADMISSION evidence for T14 and T15 says the sentence "puts back the author's own point that Emulate dropped" and "puts back the author's words or meaning", which does not describe this change (it is Emulate's sentence word for word, nothing put back).
